record_reviews.summary: Darwin sends Dana an abstract copy of Origin and asks him to read it straight through before judging the mutability thesis. The letter sets out Darwin's method of testing common descent against competing facts, his nineteen-year pigeon work, and his request for observations on whether breeds change between Europe and other regions.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML sent date is 1859-11-11, within the endpoint. The body gives no receipt date for Dana's copy and does not identify a preceding incoming question.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin's voice is continuous. Dana's views are reported and challenged in Darwin's own prose; the editorial footnotes and excluded salutation are not evidence of a Dana body.

evidence.quote: I have sent you a copy of my Book (as yet only an abstract) on the Origin of species.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin answers news of Dana's illness with a detailed water-cure recommendation, an account of his own stomach and fatigue symptoms, and advice not to read Origin while convalescing. He reports the book's unexpectedly strong reception and attacks, while inviting Dana to stay in England if he travels.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML sent date is 1859-12-30, beyond the 24 November 1859 research endpoint even though the packet retains it as a boundary/context probe. The body says Dana's illness news arrived in a letter, but supplies no surviving incoming text or receipt date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the sole authorial voice; the medical advice and book-reception claims are first-person. Dana's letter is referred to but not preserved here.

evidence.quote: You must not think of reading my book for a long time, as my friends tell me it is tough reading.

record_reviews.summary: This affectionate Moor Park letter proposes that Emma spend a fortnight taking hydropathy and reassures her about the children. Darwin then reports his possible discovery of a rare slave-making ant sent to the British Museum, his reading of two novels, and Charlotte's burnt note.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML sent date is 1858-04-25. 'Yesterday' and 'today' are internal relative markers; they do not create a separate incoming source or prove when Emma read the letter.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin's first-person voice is clear; the ant identification and novel judgments are his own, while Charlotte's note is only mentioned and explicitly burnt.

evidence.quote: I have great hopes I have found the rare Slave-making species & have sent a specimen to Brit. Mus. to know whether it is so.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin's 28 April note is a scene report from Moor Park: a walk among Scotch firs, birches, birds, squirrels and woodpeckers followed by a nap. He then reviews a novel, sketches the Hungarian exile and other acquaintances, and closes with family love; the natural-history line is an incidental joke, not a scientific exchange.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML sent date is 1858-04-28. The body uses 'Yesterday' and 'today' only for Darwin's own health and walk chronology; no incoming letter is dated or acknowledged.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin speaks throughout, with reported conversation from Mrs Lane about novels. No Emma prose survives in this record.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No identifiable incoming prompt: the source is a personal outgoing diary-like report, and the Hungarian observations are social description rather than an answer to a preserved question.

evidence.quote: I did not care one penny how any of the beasts or birds had been formed.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks James Egan, identified in the editorial apparatus against the printed 'James Egasy', for Hungarian horse-colour evidence. The body narrows the inquiry from dorsal, shoulder and leg stripes to whether stripes are clearer in foals or adults and whether dun colour follows particular parents. The separate CD note expands the enquiry to asses and mules, including transverse leg stripes and shoulder-stripe disappearance; it is Darwin's drafting note, not Egan's answer.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML sent date is 1858-11-08 with a same-day postmark. No received date or Egan response is preserved.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored both the letter and the separate CD question note; printed Gardeners' Chronicle material and Dr Lindley's role are reported context. The addendum's 'James Egasy' hotel address is an editorial/physical identification issue, not a second correspondent.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The request is Darwin-initiated. No surviving Egan incoming source in this packet identifies an answer.

evidence.quote: But what I most want to know, & which I have in vain endeavoured to find out, is whether such stripes are plainer in the foal or in the full-grown horse.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Egan for promptly making enquiries about striped horses and asks especially for further information about the foal. He separately relays Lindley's answer to Darwin's earlier query and Lindley's wish for reports on Hungarian horticulture, climate, Tokay wine and tobacco. Thus the surviving note confirms an Egan answer existed but does not preserve its wording.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML sent date is 1858-11-25. 'Immediately on receipt of your letter' establishes Darwin's receipt before this composition, but no dispatch, arrival or reading date for Egan's missing letter is supplied.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin's body is wholly his own; Egan's information and Lindley's answer are summarized, not quoted as surviving source bodies.

evidence.quote: Should you hear anything further, more especially in regard to the Foal, perhaps you will have the great kindness to communicate with me.

record_reviews.summary: Emma reports that Darwin's two Monday letters about Anne are better and that the previous four days suggest progressive improvement. She discusses bowel symptoms, possible chloroform, family travel and Malvern, then adds Wednesday corrections about the returned note and Elizabeth's arrival. It is an intimate, multi-day continuation, not a response to the later death notice.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML range is 1851-04-22 to 1851-04-23. The Wednesday additions are explicitly separated inside the source; the packet's later 1851 context does not move them to 23 April alone.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Emma is the author. Catherine, Susan, Elizabeth and other family members are reported; no Darwin body is embedded beyond the references to his Monday letters.

evidence.quote: Your 2 letters of Monday are certainly better.

record_reviews.summary: Emma's pre-post note says Darwin's Monday letter made her hopeful and gives practical suggestions for Anne's food, including rice gruel, whey and egg yolk. She reports Elizabeth's visit and family reactions, then appends an after-postscript beginning 'Alas my own' that turns to the impending loss. Fanny and Caroline's words are embedded quotations, so they remain reported voices rather than Emma's own observations.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML date is 1851-04-23, before post time, with an after-post addition. The source does not establish when Darwin read it or that it answered his later same-day death notice.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Emma authored the body; Fanny, Caroline, Etty and others appear as quoted or reported correspondents. The Fanny material is not a separate Darwin prompt.

evidence.quote: The oftener I read over your letter of Monday the more hopeful it made me.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin tells Emma that Fanny's note may have prepared her, then records Anne's death at noon, her peaceful final sleep, the daguerreotype and his own stomach illness. The closing asks Emma to rely on their mutual tenderness. It is a compact death notice sent from Malvern.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML date is 1851-04-23 at Malvern. The internal noon death time is distinct from composition, dispatch and Emma's later receipt.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the complete surviving body. Fanny's note is mentioned as an earlier message, but its full text is not this source.

evidence.quote: She went to her final sleep most tranquilly, most sweetly at 12 oclock today.

record_reviews.summary: Emma infers Anne's death from receiving no message on the previous day, explains how hope vanished, and asks Darwin not to travel hurriedly or remain alone. Midway through P1 she states that Darwin's letter has just arrived and gives her some hope of seeing him; the following consolation and family details therefore answer the death notice only after its receipt.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML date is 1851-04-24 before noon. The phrase 'Your letter is just come' is a receipt marker within the letter, not the composition date of 1412 or proof of a same-day earlier arrival.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Emma is the author. Her references to Fanny, Catherine, Miss Th. and Willy are reported family voices; no later editorial prose is part of her answer.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Same correspondent or nearby subject considered, but the preserved source is an earlier/later boundary record or a distinct outgoing letter; it cannot supply the missing incoming body.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin's long Dana letter thanks him for a Geological Development paper and a 28 November letter, debates continental antiquity, refrigeration and infertility, and describes his own species argument. He reports Gray, Lubbock and Huxley, then a postscript says he has received Dana's 8th note that morning: Cave Rat evidence, embryological/palaeontological parallelism, Chthamalus and pigeon breeds. The two Dana inputs are discussed in distinct sections and neither full incoming body is preserved here.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML date is 1856-12-21, outside 1858-1859 and retained only as earlier context. 'This morning' dates receipt relative to composition, not Dana's dispatch or reading by Darwin.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored all retained paragraphs; Dana's views and notes are paraphrased/reported. No Dana voice is reconstructed from the editorial summary.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No current-period edge. The letter is an earlier knowledge witness for Dana material but the antecedent 28 November and 8 December notes are not packet sources.

evidence.quote: This morning I have received your note of the 8th, & very much obliged I am for it.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Dana a sharply defined comparative question: whether southern temperate crustaceans resemble northern temperate forms more than Arctic resembles Antarctic forms. He requests a sentence grounded in Dana's Memoir, then discusses Purbeck mammal and lizard fossils, Owen's one-character mammal classification and his own work. The actual answer is supplied by Dana in 2083, not by any catalogue adjacency.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML date is 1857-04-05, outside the current period. Darwin's request is composed and sent on that date; no receipt date for Dana is asserted.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the sole author; Richard Owen, Lyell, Barrande, Asa Gray and others are reported third-party voices.

evidence.quote: Now I shd. very much like to know how this is with Crustaceans.

record_reviews.summary: Dana answers Darwin's crustacean comparison in ten paragraphs. He limits the Antarctic catalogue, compares Fuegian genera such as Serolis, Halicarcinus, Lithodes and Eurypodius with northern analogues, discusses Hippolyte and Crangon and rejects any known identical cold-temperate north/south species. He also reports Stimpson's 900 crustacean species, comments on the Purbeck discovery and invites further enquiries. This is a substantive response, not a generic same-topic continuation.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML date is 1857-04-27. Dana says Darwin's last letter and a former letter remain unanswered, but does not give a receipt date beyond that correspondence sequence.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Dana authored the body; Dr Eights, Kinahan, Bell, Agassiz, Stimpson and Lyell are explicitly reported authorities. The catalogue and publication references are not Dana's direct observations in every instance.

alternative_candidates_considered.assessment: Same correspondent or nearby subject considered, but the preserved source is an earlier/later boundary record or a distinct outgoing letter; it cannot supply the missing incoming body.

evidence.quote: On the point on which you enquire, I can only say we need facts.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin explicitly thanks Dana for answering the Arctic/Antarctic crustacean question, says he was curious about the point, and then discusses the US expedition, Stimpson, Huxley, Lubbock and Lyell. The first paragraph is an identifiable response to Dana's 27 April answer; the remainder is news and thanks, not a new scientific prompt.
record_reviews.date_assessment: XML date is 1857-05-25, outside the period. 'Trouble ... in answering my question' confirms Darwin had read Dana's answer before composition, but does not independently date the earlier receipt.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin authored the body and refers back to Dana's information. Huxley, Lubbock and Lyell are third-party reports.

issues.issue: Editorial apparatus uses printed/addressee form “James Egasy” while XML authority is James Egan; CD question note expands beyond the five body paragraphs and must retain its Darwin-note provenance.
Acknowledged incoming Egan letter and Lindley answer are both summarized but not preserved as packet bodies.
